items.title: Half Japanese’s David Fair Dead At 74
items.summary:
David Fair, who co-founded the experimental rock band Half Japanese with his brother Jad Fair in the mid-1970s, has died at 74. Thick Syrup Records, the label David ran in the late 2000s, and filmmaker Jeff Feuerzeig, a longtime friend who directed the 1993 documentary Half Japanese: The Band That Would Be King, announced his death on social media Sunday morning. Jad Fair told Rolling Stone that the cause was cancer, and posted a childhood photo of the two brothers on Facebook, where friends have been leaving condolences.

The Fair brothers started the band as a bedroom project after moving from Michigan to Uniontown, Maryland. In the earliest years they swapped instruments and vocal duties freely before Jad settled into the frontman role, and together they arrived at a sound that was deliberately unschooled, noisy and childlike, and full of lo-fi rock songs that stuck in the ear despite themselves.

Half Japanese issued their debut EP, Calling All Girls, in 1977, and followed it in 1980 with the triple LP 1/2 Gentlemen/Not Beasts. The lineup widened over time to include underground figures such as Don Fleming and Kramer, and the band put out a long run of records, some of them released with help from the magician Penn Jillette, a fan.

David Fair left the group in 1987 but never entirely stepped away, returning at various points across its life and recording a number of albums with Jad outside the Half Japanese catalog. He was not in the band during its highest-profile stretch in 1993, when Kurt Cobain invited Half Japanese to open for Nirvana on tour.

He rejoined for the 2014 album Overjoyed, the band's first record in more than a decade and the start of its late-period return.

items.title: Why John Galliano canceled his Met retrospective
items.summary:
John Galliano and the Metropolitan Museum of Art have called off a planned retrospective of the designer's work, a joint decision reached after sustained backlash to the exhibition's announcement over antisemitic and racist remarks Galliano made in 2011. The cancellation also means the Met Gala will get a new theme for next year.

In a statement posted to Instagram, Galliano thanked Met director Max Hollein, Costume Institute curator Andrew Bolton and Anna Wintour, and said he had decided "with great sadness" that the show should not go forward now. "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry," he wrote, adding that he did not want the argument around him to place the museum in a difficult position or to overshadow the Costume Institute's work. He also said he recognized that an exhibition honoring his work "would be painful for some."

The FADER reported that the cancellation landed a day after The New York Times ran a front-page story on the criticism the show had drawn, including donors threatening to pull or withhold gifts to the museum. Met officials had contacted Jewish community leaders about Galliano's repentance and the proposed exhibition before announcing it publicly, and the retrospective was to have addressed the 2011 remarks directly.

Galliano's career collapsed that year after he was arrested for making antisemitic and anti-Asian remarks while drunk at a Paris bar, and after tabloids published video of him saying "I love Hitler." Dior dismissed him, and a French tribunal convicted him of public hate speech. He attributed the behavior at the time to addiction to alcohol, sleeping pills and tranquilizers.

After rehab and several years out of public view, Galliano became creative director of Maison Margiela in 2014 and held the post for a decade. He told WWD in 2016 that in the intervening years, "I couldn't pick up a pencil for four years. The two things just didn't work. I couldn't. I hadn't forgiven myself."

Had it proceeded, the show would have made Galliano only the third living designer given a Costume Institute retrospective, after Yves Saint Laurent and Rei Kawakubo. According to the Times, the museum had floated the idea as early as 2010 but only began developing it after his widely praised Spring 2024 collection for Margiela.

items.title: Dolly Parton Estate Sets Two-Day DollyFests for Nashville and London in 2027, Says These ‘Parties of a Lifetime’ Will Take the Place of a Public Memorial
items.summary:
The Dolly Parton estate has announced its first large-scale public tributes to the late singer: two-day festivals called DollyFest: The Celebration of a Lifetime, to be held in Nashville and London on consecutive weekends in 2027. Specific dates have not been set.

The Nashville event was already in the works before Parton's death. Danny Nozell, her longtime business partner and the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the original plan was a multi-artist show on her 80th birthday, Jan. 19, 2026, with Parton performing and hosting. "We had the venue booked and we had the announcement ready to go," he said. "And then, in August 2025, Dolly had to take a step back after her initial health challenges."

Rather than scrap the idea, the estate has expanded it into a two-continent event, adding the London dates and pushing the whole thing to 2027. Nozell framed the decision in Parton's own terms: "A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DollyFest is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)."

As Variety reported, the festivals will effectively stand in for a public memorial service. "As far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted," Nozell said, adding that the estate would "take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly."

The estate said it is not discouraging other tributes this fall, and expects many, but that DollyFest represents its official commemoration. Nozell said the delay also gives fans and artists time to grieve and to plan. Further details on both festivals are expected soon.

items.title: Ariana Grande Has to Wear “Cozy Footwear” During Final London Shows After Suffering “Minor Injury”
items.summary:
Ariana Grande will finish her Eternal Sunshine Tour in flat shoes. The singer told fans on her Instagram Story Monday that a foot injury will keep her out of her usual heels for the last two shows of her run at London's The O2, on Monday and Tuesday.

"I wanted to let you know I will need to be in cozy footwear for this evening's show (and possibly tomorrow's) as I am bandaged up underneath, recovering from a minor injury," she wrote, clarifying that it "is not a sprain or anything muscular but just a deep cut!" She warned that she might have "a little trouble putting weight on that foot" and told fans not to worry: "On with the show and I am on the mend!"

The post followed fan videos circulating online from Friday night's London date, in which Grande appeared to be limping as the show ended. The Hollywood Reporter noted the clips preceded her explanation.

The Eternal Sunshine Tour began in June and has taken Grande across North America and Europe, closing with a ten-night residency at The O2. She released her eighth studio album, Petal, at the end of July.

When the tour wraps Tuesday, Grande plans to step back from public-facing work after a year of heavy online commentary about her health and appearance. She addressed the break at a Chicago show, saying it was "not a reactive or impulsive thing. It was something that I have decided. A plan that I had quietly made a long time ago. It was a decision that was made from a thoughtful and empowered place."

items.title: HBO Max To Launch In Japan As Hub Within Prime Video & Hulu
items.summary:
Warner Bros. Discovery is bringing HBO Max to Japan, but not as a standalone app. The company said Monday it has signed deals with Amazon's Prime Video and with Hulu Japan to launch HBO Max as branded hubs inside both services starting Oct. 1.

The arrangement gives Japanese subscribers access to House of the Dragon, The Pitt, The Last of Us, The White Lotus, Euphoria, The Penguin, Peacemaker, Lanterns, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms and Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, along with films including Barbie and One Battle After Another. Upcoming titles include the forthcoming Harry Potter series. Until now, HBO and HBO Max programming reached Japan only through a licensing deal with U-Next.

Hulu Japan is a separate company from the Disney-controlled U.S. service and is owned by Nippon Television. As part of that agreement, Deadline reported, WBD and Nippon TV will look at distributing Nippon and Hulu Japan local productions on HBO Max internationally.

James Gibbons, WBD's president for Asia-Pacific, said the deals "enable us to broaden the distribution of HBO Max in Japan, which has seen a strong increase in engagement and awareness since launch." He singled out the Harry Potter series as a draw, calling it "an IP that is incredibly popular with Japanese fans."

The hub model lets WBD reach Japanese viewers through platforms that already have subscribers rather than building an audience from scratch, and it arrives ahead of the Harry Potter launch. The rollout begins Oct. 1.
